newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean president's son begs forgiveness.
newsitem.headline: South Korean president's son begs forgiveness.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam's son, embroiled in accusations he traded favours and meddled in state affairs, on Monday apologised and said he was ready for punishment if he had done wrong.
Kim Hyun-chul, in begging forgiveness, made no mention of the loans scandal involving failed Hanbo Steel Co to which his name has been linked.
His father apologised for the scandal on television last month, saying he felt shame that his son had been dragged into the affair.

On Monday, the trial began of a former cabinet minister, the founder of the Hanbo Group and eight other people in connection with billions of dollars of improper loans to the country's second-biggest steel-maker.
The opposition alleges that Kim Hyun-chul, who holds no official post, peddled influence to help win loans for Hanbo. They also accuse him of playing a key role in administration appointments.
"Lowering my head, I deeply apologise to the people and solicit forgiveness," a statement from the president's second son said. He did not admit to any crime.
"I also apologise to my father for my failure to fulfil my filial duty as a son."
"I wanted to help my father but as a consequence made the mistake of causing trouble to father and anxiety to the people. I am deeply repentant now," the statement said.
He said he "wept profusely" during his father's apology over the scandal involving $5.8 billion in loans to Hanbo, which folded in January.
State prosecutors exonerated Kim Hyun-chul in a probe into Hanbo's collapse, but the opposition slammed the investigation as a whitewash and demanded a new inquiry.
Kim Hyun-chul said he was prepared to testify before parliament and would agree to a new prosecution probe into his role in the Hanbo affair.
"I will willingly accept any punishment if I was in the wrong," he said.
Meanwhile, the trial of 10 people charged over the Hanbo collapse opened in a Seoul criminal court.
Former home affairs minister Kim Woo-suk has been charged with bribery.
Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo faces charges of embezzling 213.6 billion won ($243 million), fraud, issuing bad cheques and violating laws on trust and savings companies.

Also in the dock on corruption charges were three top bankers, four legislators -- three of them close Kim aides and one from the opposition -- and Chung's chief accountant, who was also charged with embezzlement.
All defendants were dressed in pale blue prison garb.

Former minister Kim admitted taking up to 200 million won ($227,000) from Hanbo's Chung, but not as a bribe. The cash was stashed in a crate covered with apples and placed in the trunk of his car while the two were at dinner, he said.
All three bankers acknowledged they, too, had received money from Chung hidden in apple crates.
The opposition legislator, Kwon Rho-kap, said Chung handed him a locked bag stuffed with 50 million won in notes while the two dined in a guest room at Seoul's Grand Hyatt Hotel.

Kwon said as he left the room with the bulging bag, two bellboys spotted him. He panicked and returned the money to the room. The cash was later handed to him by Chung in a night rendevous outside the national theatre.
